cards.text: This psalm doesn't say who wrote it, but it opens with a call to sing to the LORD a new song. A NEW one, friend. Not the same tune I hum at my ovens every single morning, the one even the dough is sick of hearing.

cards.question: The psalm calls for a new song to the LORD. What reason does it give?

cards.text: The psalm also talks about a victory. And it is VERY clear about who won it.

cards.question: True or false: The psalm says Israel's army gained the LORD the victory.

cards.text: His own right hand and holy arm gained Him the victory. My mustache has packed a LOT of cookie boxes, friend, but it has never won anything bigger than a staring contest with the oven.

cards.question: The psalm goes on: the LORD has ___ His salvation and revealed His righteousness to the nations.

cards.text: Then the psalm says He has remembered His love and faithfulness to the house of Israel. Friend, I set an oven timer, walk FIVE steps away, and forget I even OWN an oven.

cards.question: True or false: The psalm says only the house of Israel has seen the salvation of our God.

cards.text: Now the psalm turns a corner. It's done telling what the LORD did, and it starts handing out invitations.

cards.question: The psalm starts calling for praise to the LORD. Who is it calling on?
True or false: The psalm wants this praise to the LORD kept soft and quiet.

cards.text: A joyful NOISE, friend, not a perfect one, which is GREAT news for my singing voice. Then the psalm brings in the band, starting with the lyre and the harp.

cards.question: After the lyre and the harp, the psalm turns the volume UP. What joins in next?
The psalm calls everyone to shout for joy before the LORD, the King. True or false: It calls on more than people, and invites the sea and all that fills it too.

cards.text: Then the psalm says, 'Let the rivers clap their hands,' and I need you to picture that. RIVERS. Clapping. Friend, whoever's sitting in the front row for THAT applause is going home SOAKED.

cards.question: The rivers aren't the only part of creation the psalm calls on. What else does it call to sing together for joy?
The psalm calls the rivers and the mountains to rejoice before the LORD, the King. What reason does it give?

answers.text: He comes to judge the earth
He sends rain on the land
He made them by His hand

cards.text: Judgment might sound like the scary part. But this psalm calls all of creation to rejoice about it, and I think it's because of HOW He judges.

cards.question: The LORD is coming to judge, and the psalm calls creation to celebrate instead of tremble. What does it say about how He judges?

cards.text: Righteousness for the world, equity for the peoples. A Judge who's fair to EVERYBODY? Friend, that's not polite clapping from those rivers anymore, that's a STANDING OVATION.

findings.problem: The blank asks for the exact BSB word "proclaimed," which has not appeared in any earlier card. Although the alternatives make one choice more plausible, the card is still testing wording the baker has not seen rather than a meaning established by the setup.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The second half of verse 3 is handled only by negating the statement that Israel alone has seen God's salvation. No card supplies the positive detail that all the ends of the earth have seen it, leaving an important part of the verse's worldwide scope unstated.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: This non-opening story card uses four separate sentences or emphatic sentence fragments: the setup, "RIVERS.", "Clapping.", and the final punchline. It exceeds the two-sentence limit and can be consolidated without losing the joke.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.
